This is NPR News Now. The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Charles Snyder. Israelis are voting today. Polls began opening a few hours ago in Israel's first national vote since the October 7th attacks and the war in Gaza.
Tens of thousands of Israelis have flown home to cast ballots. They include Omar Maraire. She was among those who flew into Israel's Ben Gurion airport from Greece.

Polls show an extremely tight race that threatens Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's hold on power.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio says it will take time to get to legitimate elections in Venezuela.
And Piers Michele Kellerman reports on his comments a day after a leading opposition figure returned to Venezuela to a hero's welcome.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio says he only once personally encouraged Nobel Peace Prize winner Maria Carina Machado not to return to Venezuela.
That was in the aftermath of back-to-back deadly earthquakes. But he says he did call on the interim authorities to make sure she could return.
And I mean weeks and weeks ago, we spoke to the interim authorities and just said, look, our expectation is that she's a Venezuelan. She belongs in her country.
That's the country she's from. She should be allowed to return. She should be allowed to return unperturbed.
Rubio says the goal of his diplomacy is to reform the electoral system so that Venezuela can become, in his words, an enduring republic.
He doesn't give a timeline for elections. Michelle Kellerman, NPR News, the State Department.
Russia and Ukraine say they have begun to localize ceasefire in the Russian-occupied town of Oleshki in southern Ukraine.
The ceasefire is aimed at allowing aid deliveries and evacuations.
So White House said last week that First Lady Melania Trump helped secure the Oleshki ceasefire.
Some coastal areas in southern California flooded Monday and will continue to be at risk in the coming days.
Warm ocean temperatures are in part to blame for an exceptionally high tide. Joe Wecklogel, Member Station, LAS, reports from Newport Beach.
The Balboa Peninsula is a thin strip of land between the ocean and Newport Harbor, filled with homes and businesses.
The city sent employees to pump water to prevent streets and homes from flooding.
It mostly worked, except for streets like this one, where one homeowner refused to place sandbags along her seawall.
Neighbor Diane Teichyde was trying to keep cars from sloshing the water into people's garages.
The city's been great about making sandbags available. There's no excuse not to have them.
Newport Beach could start fining residents who don't take precautions against flooding.
Even higher tide is expected in the coming days.
For NPR News, I'm Jill Repplogel in Newport Beach.
And you're listening to NPR News.
The artificial intelligence giant, Anthropik, has filed paperwork for what could be the biggest initial public offering of stock ever.
Monday's filings set up the company, based in San Francisco, for a Wall Street debut next month, putting it ahead of rival OpenAI and going public.
A manhunt is underway in Tennessee. Authorities are looking for a convicted murderer who escaped from a prison in northwest Tennessee.
Officials say 28-year-old Jacob Morley was discovered missing late Sunday at the northwest correctional complex.
To Australia now, where a convicted killer has lost his legal bid to overturn a ban on the breakfast spread vegemite in prison.
Christina Cocuglia reports from Melbourne on a case that drew international attention when the prisoner argued the ban had breached his human rights.
Andrew McKechnie is serving a life sentence in prison for murder.
Appearing before the Supreme Court in the state of Victoria, he argued the vegemite ban violated his right to enjoy his culture as an Australian and made him feel sad and disconnected from his family and community.
In dismissing the case, the court said denying him access to the salty, yeast-based breakfast spread was reasonable and "demonstrably justified".
The judge noted there are other ways for prisoners to enjoy Australian culture, including through local music and books.
Vegemite, a staple in Australian homes, was banned in Victorian prisons 20 years ago.
Due to concerns, it could obstruct drug detection and be used to brew alcohol.
For NPR News, I'm Christina Cocuglia in Melbourne.
And I'm Giles Snyder. This is NPR News.
